events.title: Electricity discount to be paid to NI households
events.summary: The one-off reduction will be paid from next month Published 17 September 2026, 00:01 BST All households in Northern Ireland will get a one-off £63 reduction in electricity bills from next month. It is the local outworking of two schemes which apply in Great Britain, which has a separately regulated electricity market. The schemes are being funded by the UK government and will be applied automatically without the need for an application. Bank payment customers will have their bills automatically reduced while pay-as-you-go customers will receive £63 in credit when they top up their meter. The only complication for pay-as-you-go customers is they should not buy more than £112 of credit if they want to get the discount all in one go. That is because meters are set up to take a maximum payment of £175. Top ups over this value means the £63 payment will be split over a subsequent top up. Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said the money would help families The Economy Minister Dr Caoimhe Archibald said the money would "provide some help for families as winter kicks in and energy bills rise". She said the money would "provide some help for families as winter kicks in and energy bills rise". Her department agreed the NI scheme with the government and will deliver it to consumers. Last week applications opened for a separate means-tested scheme to provide a £100 voucher to some heating oil users. It is jointly funded by Stormont and the UK government. The electricity scheme reflects two policies which apply in GB: a temporary cut in VAT and the removal of some consumer levies. The UK government decided not to apply the VAT cut in NI as it would have required agreement with the EU which it thought would lead to delay. There are due to be similar bill reductions in the next two years but the size of those will depend on whether the government continues with the VAT cut which was introduced as a temporary measure. It comes as energy prices continue to rise, driven by the US conflict with Iran. Data from the NI consumer council suggests 500 litres of home heating oil currently costs around £560, more than twice the price compared to this time last year. events.title: Trump says U.S. ‘hopefully’ nearing end of Iran war as Saudi Arabia-Houthis trade strikes
events.summary: Trump says the U.S. may be nearing the end of its nearly seven-month war with Iran, as he signals Tehran is open to a deal. The conflict is expanding into Yemen, with Iran-backed Houthis escalating attacks on Saudi Arabia and seeking control of the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Gulf economies and oil markets face mounting pressure, with Saudi Arabia racing to repair a crucial crude pipeline as analysts warn of a prolonged supply disruption. U.S. President Donald Trump has said the country is "hopefully" toward the end of its nearly seven-month war with Iran, as fighting continues to escalate between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. "Well, hopefully we are toward the end of the war. They want to make a deal, we'll see how that works out," Trump told reporters in North Carolina on Wednesday evening. The U.S. president also said he had spoken with Tehran "directly," without providing further details. His comments come as the sprawling Middle East conflict, which started on Feb. 28, expands into Yemen, further disrupting energy exports and rattling oil markets . The Houthis have ramped up attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia and launched a lightning ground offensive to exercise control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a vital oil choke point that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and to global markets. Trump is planning to meet Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York next Tuesday to discuss next steps for the war with Iran, Axios reported Thursday. The report came as Washington's efforts to resume ceasefire talks appear to have stalled, as Gulf states absorb escalating attacks from Iran and Iran-aligned Houthi militants in recent days. Trump is expected to meet leaders from the six Gulf Cooperation Council states — Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman — with the guest list possibly widening to other Arab and Muslim leaders, according to the report. The State Department sent initial invitations Wednesday, Axios reported, citing unnamed people with knowledge of the matter. The discussion will focus on U.S. proposals for a postwar strategy, Axios reported, as Trump and his senior team work on a day-after plan that isn't expected to be finalized until after the U.S. midterm elections in November. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also wants to meet Trump in New York, though no meeting has been scheduled, according to the report, which cited an Israeli source. The latest diplomatic push comes as Gulf states face mounting economic costs from the conflict. Saudi Arabia shut its East-West Pipeline , a highly strategic network that transports crude oil from the kingdom's eastern coast to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, following the damage caused by a drone attack. Oil prices were traded lower on Thursday after Saudi Arabia reportedly arranged additional shipments through Oman's Sohar port via ship-to-ship transfers, easing fears of a prolonged supply gap. International benchmark Brent crude futures with November expiry fell 1.5% to $104.28 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures with October expiry dipped 1.1% to $101.30. On Wednesday, U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres repeated calls for de-escalation in the region, urging diplomacy and the restoration of freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz. It remains unclear what Washington would require of Gulf states or Iran postwar. Iran could be open to negotiating after the U.S. midterms, but continued reluctance to engage diplomatically risks dragging the conflict out for longer, said Michael Feller, chief strategist at Geopolitical Strategy. "Iran may be willing to do a deal after the midterms. If not, the war may continue until late 2028, if not beyond," Feller said. One source of relief would be repairs to the East-West Pipeline, he said, though export-terminal stockpiles will run out unless the line is restored within days.

events.title: Next forecasts bigger profits after hot weather lifts sales
events.summary: FTSE 100 retailer, which owns UK rights to US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret, says prices could rise in autumn Next has thanked warmer weather for an “unexpected” boost in sales, leading the clothing retailer to raise its profit forecasts for the fourth time this year. The FTSE 100 company, which owns the UK rights to the US brands Gap and Victoria’s Secret as well as stakes in labels including Reiss and Joules, raised its expectations for full-year profits by £12m to £1.26bn. It is the fourth time Next has raised profit forecasts this year, with the company having last ratcheted up its expectations in early August , as Europe faced a series of heatwaves . Next, which has more than 500 stores across the UK, said in a stock market update on Thursday: “The first half was much better than we originally anticipated, both in the UK and overseas. “It is important to acknowledge that part of this overperformance has been the result of two unusually warm summers in the UK. The rest of the overperformance is, we believe, largely the result of fulfilling the aims we outlined at the beginning of the year.” That has included some cost-cutting efforts, particularly across Next’s warehouses. Overall, total sales across the group were up 9% in the six months to July, helping push pre-tax profits for the half-year up by 11% to £566m. Next said the performance over the past six months was “all the more unexpected given the strength of sales last year”. It made £1bn of annual profits for the first time last year. However, the retailer cautioned on the impact of the rising cost of living and prospects for the jobs market. “Our primary concerns are rising inflation, higher mortgage interest costs and a weak employment market. These worries will only be compounded if they are accompanied by tax increases,” it said, in an apparent reference to John Healey’s first budget on 28 October. “It seems likely that it [the government] will have to increase taxes in order to fund its expenditure.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning While the group said it was deploying AI across the business, including its tech division, Next said it was ensuring fashion designs were still led by humans. “In a world where AI is able to do more and more, our experience suggests that consumers prefer the authentic creativity of human beings,” it said. “That means we are putting more emphasis on designers using techniques that connect them directly to the artwork – painting, drawing, screen printing, etc. That is a big investment in time, and requires a higher level of creative talent than is needed to operate CAD [computer aided design] or prompt AI.” Aarin Chiekrie, an equity analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown, said: “Next delivered its first-half results in style, with sales growth accelerating over the period and breezing past the fashion company’s original guidance. In the UK, hotter-than-expected weather and more effective marketing saw customers logging in to refresh their summer wardrobes online, helping offset a small decline in-store.”

events.title: India warns new US tariffs over Russian oil could impact ties
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections New Delhi says it has ‘made clear’ its determination to ‘protect its trade and economic interests’. India has warned the United States that new measures to levy tariffs over the purchase of Russian oil could impact ⁠bilateral ties, hours after the US Congress approved a bill that would give President Donald Trump new abilities to punish buyers of Russian oil. The US House of Representatives on Wednesday passed a sweeping sanctions and tariff bill intended to increase economic pressure on Russia over its invasion of ⁠Ukraine. list 1 of 3 BRICS summit: What are the key takeaways? list 2 of 3 BRICS meets in India: What’s on the agenda, why it matters list 3 of 3 How US Senate Russia sanctions could spell 100% tariffs for India, China The bill targets Russia’s energy and defence sectors, President Vladimir Putin and other senior officials, as well as Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet of tankers used to circumvent Western sanctions. It also authorises President Donald Trump to impose stiff tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries, including India, to reduce their dependence on Russian oil and gas, and⁠ extend sanctions on Iran. The bill has been sent to Trump to sign into law. India’s foreign ministry said on Thursday that it “remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people”. The Indian foreign ministry said that it had noted the bill’s passage, adding that New Delhi had raised the issue with various US interlocutors in recent months, and had “very clearly articulated” the potential implications for the bilateral relationship and the international energy market. “The Indian side has also made clear its determination to take all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests,” it said in a statement. The government would work closely with trade and industry bodies to deal with the legislation’s implications, it added. India, the world’s third-biggest oil importer, is among the biggest buyers of Russian oil , which is seen as helping Moscow replenish its budget since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and was hit with ⁠sweeping Western sanctions. New Delhi has repeatedly sought to resist pressure to reduce its oil trade with Russia, saying its large population and economy need secure, affordable and reliable energy supplies.

events.title: ACT schools grappling with class 'splitting', as union flags more industrial action
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Frequent class 'splitting' disrupting Canberra students, as union flags further industrial action The Australian Education Union said the government had not provided enough detail on minimum staffing guarantees in its latest offer. ( ABC News: Adam Shirley ) Teachers are set to stop work again next week after the union says a pay and conditions offer from the government failed to meet their demands. Inadequate resourcing and workforce shortages have led to cases where one teacher is managing up to 90 kids due to class 'splitting' and 'collapsing', the union says. One issue raised is a lack of streamlined reporting on workforce shortages, which the ACT's Education Directorate says it is addressing. The Australian Education Union's ACT branch is predicting teachers and other school staff will stop work again next week after what it expects will be a resounding rejection of the government's latest pay and conditions offer. Today, there was minimal supervision for ACT public school students between 9am and 11am as union members met to consider the offer. AEU ACT president Angela Burroughs said a formal response to the deal would be provided next week, but a no vote meant teachers and other school staff would most likely stop work again next Thursday morning. She said members were exhausted by "a prolonged period of inadequate resourcing" in Canberra schools and wanted a guarantee of minimum staffing levels. Angela Burroughs said teacher working conditions were influencing decisions on whether people took up the profession. ( ABC News: Monte Bovill ) Teachers managing up to 90 kids, union says Australia is grappling with a national shortage of teachers . Ms Burroughs explained the profession had become "less attractive" over time as teachers weighed up potential burnout with pay and conditions. Class 'splitting' and 'collapsing', Ms Burroughs said, was an "inevitable consequence" of teacher shortages. Splitting is described as when a teacher is unavailable, and their students are then allocated to multiple available staff. Collapsing is when the class cannot be split into groups, and so the whole class is placed with one teacher. Shortages are forcing different year groups together in one class, the union says. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke ) "We are seeing one teacher having to teach huge class sizes — 50, 90 in some instances — it has gotten completely out of hand," Ms Burroughs said. ACT public school system to be unified in 'generational shift' The ACT's public education system will be significantly changed after a review of resourcing found schools operated much like "independent small businesses". Ms Burroughs said this could lead to the "most disruptive" cases where very different year groups were mismatched. "It is really hard for the classroom teacher to be able to meet such a diverse range of needs," Ms Burroughs said. Representative body ACT Parents' Veronica Elliot said her organisation surveyed parents and carers at the beginning of 2026, which reported that splitting and collapsing was happening weekly to fortnightly. She said she had also heard of students going a year without a specialist maths teacher. Veronica Elliot said splitting and collapsing remained a big issue of parents and carers. ( ABC News: David Sciasci ) "It does disrupt learning, and we know this is having a big impact on what students are able to achieve, because they just don't have a teacher in front of them," she said. "The issue is that we really don't know how big of a problem it is, because the Education Directorate doesn't collect data on their ongoing vacancies, and also on the splitting and collapsing of classes." She said the data was needed to understand the scale of the problem. ACT Education Directorate Director-General Jo Wood said the directorate was developing a system to show how schools were being affected. ACT Education Director-General Jo Wood agreed improving data collection on workforce shortages was critical. ( ABC News: David Sciasci ) "That automated data system will be the way that we bring visibility to that issue and then we can start to work on some really concrete systems," she said. Ms Wood noted the effects of a declining casual workforce and increased use of leave in a post-COVID era, saying people were being encouraged to stay home when sick. "We're in the flu season at the moment, and we're seeing more people have to access their personal leave," she said. She said the Education Directorate had committed to working with the union and schools to better handle the issue.

events.title: Bank of England expected to slow bond-selling programme and hold interest rates today – business live
events.summary: Introduction: Bank of England to set rates and bond-selling programme Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the world economy and the financial markets. It’s a crunch day for the Bank of England . The UK central bank will announce its latest interest rate decision at noon, and also reveal whether it has made any changes to its bond-selling programme. The City are pretty confident that the Bank will leave rates on hold, at 3.75%, despite inflation rising further away from its 2% target yesterday. But while perhaps three members of the monetary policy committee might vote for a hike, they’ll probably be outvoted by the other six…. (but you never know for sure!). The problem facing the Bank of England is that it has a mandate to control inflation, but there are signs that consumers are struggling – and a rate hike would add to that pressure on households. Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, explains: The labour market is weak, payrolled employment is falling, wage growth is negative in real terms and job vacancies are also at a multi-year low. July growth was stronger than expected, however, this was driven by AI Capex spend, and construction and manufacturing contracted last month. BoE policymakers might also feel slightly uncomfortable that other central bankers have been raising rates – including the US Federal Reserve yesterday (to the annoyance of Donald Trump). As Fed chair Kevin Warsh pointed out: “The plain fact is that [US] inflation is too high, and has been for too long. “This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.” The Bank’s decision on quantitative tightening (QT) – the sale of bonds bought to stimulate the economy – is harder to call, and potentially more explosive. Economists expect the Bank to slow the pace of QT – perhaps to an annual pace of £50bn, down from £70bn over the last year. It might even halt the sale of long-dated bonds, where it has faced criticism for helping to push borrowing costs to multi-year highs. [This is because bond yields rise when prices fall, and prices are pushed down if one major bond-holder is determined to sell their gilts]. The Bank has already faced criticism from the Reform party for pressing on with QT, given the losses being incurred by taxpayers. The Guardian wrote earlier this week that QT needs to be revised, explaining: No other major central bank carries on in this way. Whatever one thinks of the losses, making the Treasury settle them immediately turns monetary choices into fiscal interventions. A report this week says that the Bank and Treasury are drawing up changes to QT to reduce pressure on raising interest rates. Independence seems to have been discarded in favour of quiet coordination. The MPC’s decisions cannot be beyond challenge. Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, calls the overall cost of QT “ neutral ” – but only, as the economist Patricia Pino points out, when assessed over six decades. In fact, billions in cash demands fall within a parliament. Governments do not set budgets, fight elections or run public services over 60 years. It is unsustainable for the Bank to make decisions and have ministers face voters for the political consequences. 10am BST: Eurozone inflation report for August 12pm BST: Bank of England decision on interest rates and QT 1.3pm BST: US initial jobless claims data 9m ago London stocks rise after Fed rate hike 1h ago Next warns of UK slowdown despite lifting profit forecast 2h ago Introduction: Bank of England to set rates and bond-selling programme London stocks rise after Fed rate hike The London stock market has opened higher, as investors shrug off last night’s US interest rate rise. If tightening remains measured, credit spreads remain stable, and profits continue to grow, the rally should have scope to broaden across sectors and regions. We recommend diversified equity exposure while avoiding excessive concentration in areas that are particularly sensitive to interest rates or rely on a single return driver.” Haefele also gives three reasons why markets might not be too rattled by the Fed: Much of the tightening is already priced in. events.title: Why Package Digital Twins Are So Hard To Build
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Package twins must track what manufacturing actually builds, not just design intent. Missing process and supplier data can undermine otherwise precise simulations. Coupled physics and ongoing calibration keep models tied to physical reality. A chiplet can be fully characterized, tested, and considered known good, but none of that guarantees it will stay that way after it’s placed into a different package. While the chiplet itself may be unchanged, nearly everything around it can move. A different substrate can alter the mechanical and electrical environment, a different thermal interface can change how heat leaves the device, and a new power envelope can increase how much heat needs to leave in the first place. A thermal path that worked in the first product can cause throttling in the second because the surrounding package and cooling assumptions have changed. By the time the chiplet is assembled into another package, engineers may be dealing with a different system altogether, which is why package models can’t stop at the die boundary, and why the added complexity makes package digital twins so difficult to achieve. That is the basic problem facing digital twins for advanced packaging. They have to predict how known components will behave after integration and eventually inside a larger system. “A chiplet may be characterized and validated in one package or product SKU, then reused in a different package stack, substrate, cooling approach, or power envelope,” said Kenneth Larsen, senior director of product management at Synopsys . “The chiplet has not changed, but its electrical, thermal, and mechanical environment has.” Fab vs. packaging: A different kind of twin Digital twins are starting to be used in semiconductor manufacturing, but the comparison with front-end fabs needs some clarification. A fab process twin can be enormously complicated, incorporating equipment behavior, process history, and statistical learning. The difference is that much of that complexity remains inside a relatively well-defined manufacturing environment. “A fab process twin is extremely complex, so I would not frame this as fab being easy and package being hard,” Larsen said. “The difference is the nature of the problem. A fab twin is usually deep within one manufacturing environment, one process technology, and one managed flow of equipment, materials, process data, and statistical learning. A package digital twin has to solve a broader integration problem — how a multi-die system is realized across silicon, substrate, assembly, manufacturing variation, test, and reliability learning.” That broader integration problem changes what the twin has to represent. In heterogeneous integration, the package is increasingly part of the system architecture, so electrical, thermal and mechanical behavior cannot be optimized independently. Engineers already have effective tools for each of those domains, but they don’t become a package twin simply by running next to one another. The harder problem is keeping them synchronized around the same physical package as it moves from design to manufacturing. Manufacturing results also need to feed back into those models as the package is revised. “The package, silicon, substrate, materials, thermal solution, and manufacturing assumptions have to be explored together,” Larsen said. “If they are optimized separately, the digital twin becomes a late-stage validation artifact. That is not where the value is.” The boundary also becomes less obvious once the package moves onto a board and into its eventual system. Conditions outside the package can change its behavior, which means some of that context has to travel with the model. “An end-to-end package digital twin requires visibility across the entire lifecycle, from wafer fabrication through assembly, test, and ultimately system operation,” said Joon Ahn, vice president of global factory IT and automation at Amkor . “Some key process information originates upstream in foundry operations or downstream in customer applications.” Preserving that context would be difficult even if all of the necessary information were sitting in one place. Often, it’s not. The data hole From the OSAT perspective, much of the information needed to describe an advanced package comes from elsewhere. Some of it comes from the foundry, some from substrate and material suppliers, and some is generated only after assembly or test. Even equipment inside the same manufacturing flow may provide different types of data depending on its age and supplier. “For OSATs, an end-to-end digital twin is not a single model, but a connected ecosystem of process, equipment, production, supply chain, and traceability data,” said Ahn. “Packaging performance is influenced by interactions among multiple process steps. Some key process information originates upstream in foundry operations or downstream in customer applications.” What an OSAT receives can be quite different from what a predictive model ideally contains. Incoming die data may include critical dimensions and wafer-sort results, but not detailed power-density or local stress maps. A substrate may arrive within nominal specifications without showing actual warpage across the production lot, while material data sheets may not capture material-specific behavior in the end device. “The downstream analysis can then look precise while missing the manufacturing reality,” Larsen said. “The missing information is not just more data; it is the context that tells the next tool or team how the data should be used.” That context can be lost even when plenty of data survives the handoff. The problem is that different parts of the supply chain may describe the same physical system in different ways. “The hardest handoffs aren’t necessarily where we have the least data. They’re usually where the data has to move between very different engineering domains,” said CP Hung, vice president of corporate R&D at ASE . “A foundry may describe die behavior one way, a substrate supplier another, and a materials company may provide properties measured under a very specific set of conditions. Then the OSAT has to bring all of that together and understand how it will behave during assembly.” That context becomes even harder to preserve when the information crosses company boundaries. The material supplier knows things about the chemistry that the equipment company doesn’t. The equipment company knows details of the process integration that may not be available to the OSAT or fab. Much of that knowledge also represents intellectual property. “We all have our own data and everybody wants to protect intellectual property,” said Sanjiv Bhatt, senior director of marketing and business development at Mitsubishi Chemical Group. “I’ve been in this industry all my life, and when we started we had a different way of collaborating. events.title: Reddit co-founder says tech industry has been 'tone deaf' in explaining AI: 'Misinformation flying around'
events.summary: Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian told CNBC the industry has been "pretty tone deaf" in explaining the risks of AI. Ohanian said the AI debate should focus on substantive risks rather than become issues used to score political points. It comes days after warnings from researchers at AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic of the rapid advancement of the technology known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI. The tech industry has been "tone deaf" in explaining AI and properly informing the public about real risks, Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian told CNBC on Wednesday. Ohanian said the debate around AI should focus on substantive risks rather than issues that can be used to score political points, arguing that an informed public is essential to navigating the technology. He acknowledged that the tech industry has contributed to the problem by doing a "pretty tone deaf job" of explaining AI, while suggesting that its risks are more mundane than the "Terminator and Skynet" scenarios some fear. Skynet is a fictional self-aware AI system in the "Terminator" movies that saw humans as a threat and sought to wipe them out. The comments come days after warnings from researchers at AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic of the rapid advancement of the technology known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI. RSI refers to AI systems helping develop more advanced models, potentially creating a cycle in which increasingly capable systems contribute to building even more capable ones. The concern is that if AI systems take over the process of training new models, their human developers could eventually lose control over how those systems evolve. Ohanian argued that while AI risks are real, apocalyptic "Terminator"-style warnings can distract from real concerns such as agent swarms, when multiple AI agents work together to perform a complicated task. "There are risks, I do think they're more benign, or they're more banal than people are thinking," he said. He compared AI to nuclear energy because both technologies are powerful scientific advances that can cause serious harm but also deliver major benefits if managed responsibly. "I'm hopeful this goes in a healthy direction, and it's just going to require fewer tweets and more, like, thoughtful conversation," Ohanian said. "The doomer tweet was discouraging," he said without specifying, adding it was "frustrating" when "the slogans are actually not real things." Earlier this month, an AI researcher quit his job at Anthropic and accused the company and OpenAI of acting irresponsibly when it comes to developing the powerful technology. Jacob Coxon, who has worked as a researcher at both companies, said on social media that he resigned because he was concerned that Anthropic and OpenAI are "gambling with our lives." He said the people building AI "earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." For Ohanian, nuance is crucial. "We should have a discussion about the important, like real stuff, instead of these things that maybe score some quick political points… I have faith that we can have this discussion." "It frustrates me because I see all this misinformation flying around, but I do think in the long run, we [will] get it right, and that's what I'm hoping happens. So I'm not terribly worried about that part of it."

events.title: Negative Expansion Materials Resist Warpage
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Warpage is becoming a bigger constraint as package, interposer, and panel sizes grow. Negative thermal expansion (NTE) materials, newly on the market, can help counter warpage. Commercial NTE materials are starting to be used in semiconductor packaging, but broader adoption will depend on temperature range, compatibility of different materials, and uniform mixing and purity. Thermally induced warpage, caused by differences in the rate at which materials expand when heated, is becoming increasingly problematic in large chips and packages. The solution may be to integrate a new class of materials that actually shrink when heated. Rather than relying solely on the few substances that can shrink, companies are focusing on mixtures of materials with a lattice structure that can resist the urge to expand. Using such materials for underfill and as the packaging molding compound can add rigidity for larger packages while keeping warpage in check. Warpage as the enemy Warpage, especially in large packages and panels, occurs because of mismatches between how, for example, a substrate, a die, and surrounding molding compound behave when heated. It’s one of the biggest issues holding back the constant enlargement of package substrates, interposers, and panels. The larger the bonded area, the greater the likelihood that edge connections may be poor or fail altogether. Even before bonding, too much warpage can defeat standard manufacturing equipment features such as vacuum chucks. “The vacuum chucks will pull the warpage down, but if the warpage is too high, then you won’t get a good vacuum,” said Knowlton Olmstead, senior manager of wafer services at Amkor . Anywhere two materials meet with different coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE), warping is likely to some degree. For example, given two layers of material, if the bottom layer has a higher CTE, then it will try to expand to its natural extent. But the material above it will restrict it, assuming they’re well adhered. That will cause the edges of the bottom material to want to curl up. It’s theoretically impossible to stop all warpage if there is a CTE difference. The question becomes how much is too much. If it’s too much, what can you do about it? “We do a certain level of modeling to model the warpage beforehand, and then there’s certain levers you can pull to control the warpage,” said Olmstead. If silicon is one of the layers (as it often is), thinning the silicon can reduce the amount of warping. “You reduce the impact of the low CTE silicon if there’s thinner silicon,” said Mike Kelly, vice president, chiplets/FCBGA integration at Amkor. “In the extreme, you can make it super thin, and then it can follow the shape of whatever I’m attached to. But that ends up being a problem, because nobody wants really thin silicon for managing high power.” Warpage also impacts how new materials may be received, such as glass. “The larger the panel you’re trying to make, the more warpage you will see,” said Lang Lin, principal product manager at Synopsys . “Today we talk about micrometers of warpage, but with glass, it could be even larger — millimeters, maybe.” One approach being explored is to identify or design materials that contract when heated, giving them a negative CTE. “Negative CTE materials could be utilized in a variety of ways to offset expansion,” said Luke Prenger, research scientist IV team lead at Brewer Science . “It might depend on why the expansion needs to be offset to begin with. For things like stress management and warpage reduction, negative CTE materials can be utilized to help better match the CTEs of different materials. An example case of this would be to add filler to a polymer material, which typically has a very high CTE compared to inorganics, to reduce the overall CTE of the polymer matrix so it is closer to that of the metal layers and other components in the device. Reducing or modulating the CTE of organic layers to be closer to the inorganic layers helps in reducing warpage and overall stress build-up in a device.” Going against the grain One of the material interfaces that results in warping is the epoxy molding compound (EMC) used for fillers and underfill. It fills all the major gaps inside the package, so when the temperature changes, it can affect everything it touches. Altering the composition of that compound can mitigate the warping. The key is changing the CTE, with a negative CTE ideal for counteracting an adjacent positive one. Alternatively, mixing a positive CTE material with a negative one can alter the overall CTE of the combination. A variety of materials can exhibit true negative thermal expansion (NTE) behavior, although it often occurs within specific temperature ranges. It may also be associated with a phase change. For example, water behaves normally above 3.98 °C, below which it moves toward freezing. Ice is famously less dense than water due to its molecular structure, and so as more of the water takes on that configuration between 3.98°C and 0°C, it expands up until the final phase transition to ice. Unlike materials exhibiting true NTE behavior, other substances may consist of normal materials encased in a lattice that restricts expansion. The structure of that lattice is important in determining how anything encased in it behaves. “The key is the structure of the filler itself,” said Sanjiv Bhatt, senior director of global marketing and business development for the semiconductor business at Mitsubishi Chemical Group. Solids may have a wide range of molecular arrangements. Whereas polymers can be amorphous, inorganic materials typically have some sort of lattice structure. Materials scientists categorize the different structures and study their rheological properties (which refers to the study of how they flow). They’ll describe lattice structures, such as house-of-cards, rigid-rod, or tetrahedral. Each of these structures behave differently and can establish rigidity in one or more dimensions. What’s within the lattice (also called a matrix or a network) can also affect the flow, and the combined NTE materials reflect such a structure — a functional material within a restraining matrix. “It’s more of a network thing than a material thing,” explained Bhatt. “Not everything will form the same network. A carbon powder forms a flocculated network. If you look at a carbon fiber network, that is a reinforcing rigid-rod network. So if you are going to put a carbon fiber into a matrix, it’s like logs in a river. If I use the logs in water, it is going to have little impact on the ability of water to flow. It will restrict it some, but the water is still going to find room between them. If I put a whole bunch of clay in the water, it will muddy it up, and it will literally restrict the water movement because now you have changed the viscosity.” Caught in a cage Such a structure, a matrix encasing another material, can restrict the te

events.title: The Silicon Heartland Wants To Be America’s Next Chip Powerhouse
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Major facility investments are driving momentum for the Midwestern semiconductor industry. Workforce development remains a major structural challenge. Quantum investment in Chicago represents a major opportunity for the regional semiconductor ecosystem. The U.S. semiconductor industry has long been concentrated in established technology and manufacturing hubs, but new investments and startup activity are helping expand the industry’s footprint across the Midwest. The prospect of a thriving Midwestern semiconductor industry has long hinged on whether semiconductor companies can leverage the region’s strong base of research institutions and available workforce, logistics, and industrial infrastructure to build a regional ecosystem. Over the last several years, that trend has gained momentum, with Intel and SK hynix bringing landmark facility investments to the Midwest, major bets on the future of quantum computing being made on the shores of Lake Michigan, and significant government investment being funneled toward semiconductor growth and startup support. Defining the Midwestern ecosystem The Midwest has undergone something of a “transformation” in recent years, with signs of a real semiconductor ecosystem beginning to materialize. “There’s always been this culture of innovation, but because a lot of the semiconductor and microelectronics work had existed on the coasts, or had been elsewhere, while the Midwest was really the heart for manufacturing, there’s been this transformation to a technology-based silicon heartland ecosystem,” said Matt Casto, CEO of Midwest Microelectronics Consortium. “New foundry capabilities are being built just north of Columbus, Ohio. Supply chain manufacturers range from water treatment capabilities to semiconductor tools. We’ve got companies in the Midwest and in the state of Ohio now that are doing material growth development. So the building blocks for semiconductor work can connect within that Midwest ecosystem through additional supply chain capabilities. Now is a generational opportunity around advanced technology, and that requires a lot more emphasis on workforce development.” The vision for this developing semiconductor ecosystem rests on a diverse technology production network that can integrate into the region’s existing manufacturing and research base. “One defining characteristic of the Midwest is its emphasis on connecting semiconductor innovation directly to manufacturing and industrial applications,” said Christopher Salomone, account management at Synopsys . “While some regions are heavily concentrated in either semiconductor design or fabrication, the Midwest is building a more integrated ecosystem that includes research institutions, advanced manufacturing, automotive technology, defense applications, and emerging semiconductor production capabilities.” One of the biggest markers of the industry’s Midwestern development has been Intel’s $28B+ “Silicon Heartland” project in suburban Central Ohio. Expected to open in the early 2030s, the facility will create 3,000 new Intel jobs in the metro Columbus area once fully operational. “Intel’s investment helped establish the Midwest as a serious contender in advanced semiconductor manufacturing and created opportunities that simply didn’t exist in this region before,” said Ted Geer, director of state government affairs for Ohio at Intel . “The Midwest has always produced exceptional engineers, researchers, and technical talent through its universities and research institutions. Too often, however, many of those graduates built their careers elsewhere. Today, students and researchers across the region can see a pathway to participate in leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing without leaving the Midwest. Organizations like MMEC are helping build on that momentum by strengthening connections between research, talent development, and the future of domestic microelectronics.” Part of the growing momentum also comes from established regional power players expanding their footprint with long-term growth in mind. “Brewer Science has been rooted in the Midwest since 1981, and our positioning isn’t incidental to the region; it’s strategic,” said Srikanth Kommu, co-CEO at Brewer Science . “We’ve demonstrated that world-class materials innovation and manufacturing can thrive outside traditional coastal hubs, which directly challenges the historical consolidation of semiconductor ecosystems. When you connect that kind of regional leadership to what we’re doing on the ground, like our acquisition of Heraeus Epurio’s semiconductor chemicals business, which brought a production facility in Dayton, Ohio, into our operations, you start to see a materials corridor forming across the Midwest that didn’t exist five years ago. Our deliberate geographic deepening through acquisitions and internal growth, from Rolla to Vichy to Springfield to now Dayton, treats our supply chain and workforce as strategic assets. This model lets us sustain margins while investing in facility upgrades, process improvements, and worker development. The manufacturers who will matter most in this region are those treating this as a 20-year investment in institutional capability, not a response to quarterly performance metrics.” Major Midwest Semiconductor Activities Recently announced, under construction, or recently broken ground | Updated September 8, 2026. events.title: Beyond Scaling: The Growing Role Of Materials Innovation In Semiconductor Manufacturing
events.summary: For decades, semiconductor progress has been defined primarily by our ability to make devices smaller, faster and more powerful. But as the industry moves deeper into the AI era, scaling is becoming increasingly dependent on something less visible: the materials that make each new generation of devices possible. This shift is already apparent across many semiconductor manufacturing trends. Advanced-node scaling is creating requirements that existing materials cannot always satisfy. AI is driving extraordinary demand for compute performance while simultaneously increasing data movement and power consumption. Electrical interconnects are approaching practical limitations, while power delivery and thermal challenges are becoming system-level constraints. As a result, the future of semiconductor manufacturing will depend not simply on optimizing existing materials, but increasingly on developing and commercializing fundamentally different ones. This is not unique to semiconductors. Across industries, materials transitions have historically enabled major technological advances—from new battery chemistries to successive generations of displays. What is changing is the speed at which those transitions are occurring. Two forces in particular are accelerating materials innovation: rapidly expanding computational capabilities and a shift from conventional supplier relationships toward deeper co-development across the technology ecosystem. For semiconductor makers, the combination could fundamentally change how advanced materials move from the laboratory into high-volume manufacturing. Computational materials development Materials development has traditionally been an experimental discipline. Researchers synthesized a candidate material, characterized it, learned from the results and repeated the process. For complex materials, synthesizing a single candidate can take weeks, making extensive physical experimentation inherently slow. Increasing computational power has changed that equation. Simulation can now take place before synthesis, allowing researchers to determine which candidates warrant physical experimentation. As models, proprietary data sets and computational resources improve, researchers can screen increasingly large numbers of candidates and identify regions of material performance that existing approaches simply cannot reach. This distinction is important. The value of computational materials development is not limited to finding a better version of an existing material. It can reveal when incremental improvement is unlikely to meet the target at all. That knowledge can shorten development cycles by enabling researchers to abandon an unproductive material path earlier and redirect resources toward a fundamentally new solution. The progression from supplementary calculation to pre-experiment screening, hyper-screening and ultimately materials AI illustrates how computing is becoming embedded throughout the discovery process. For advanced semiconductor manufacturing, this capability will become increasingly valuable. Advanced node scaling materials must satisfy multiple—and sometimes conflicting—requirements involving electrical performance, thermal behavior, mechanical properties, purity, process compatibility and manufacturability. The search space is simply becoming too large for traditional trial-and-error development alone. The next step will be combining accumulated experimental knowledge with high-performance computing, materials AI and, eventually, quantum computing. The organizations best positioned to capitalize on these tools may be those with something AI itself cannot manufacture overnight: large quantities of high-quality, proprietary materials data accumulated through decades of real-world development. Collaboration is critical Computational power alone, however, cannot solve the semiconductor industry’s materials challenges. The second major change is organizational. Semiconductor development has evolved from relatively linear customer-supplier relationships toward much more integrated collaboration among device makers, equipment companies and materials suppliers. That trend reflects the growing interdependence of process, equipment and materials performance. When a new material must work within a deposition process, interact correctly with adjacent films and ultimately deliver a specific device characteristic, optimizing it independently makes less and less sense. This argues for earlier supplier engagement and more extensive semiconductor roadmap collaboration. Instead of developing a material internally and presenting it to customers late in the process, materials suppliers can work with ecosystem partners while requirements and process architectures are still evolving. Such partnerships offer another benefit that is difficult to replicate digitally: access to tacit knowledge. Formal specifications describe what a material needs to accomplish, but engineers working together often uncover process interactions, tradeoffs and practical constraints that never appear in a data sheet. Sharing that knowledge can substantially accelerate development. It may also require changing how development resources are allocated. Traditional risk-reduction models increase investment gradually as technical uncertainty declines. A partnership-driven approach does nearly the opposite: it commits greater resources earlier, creating enough differentiated material candidates to engage partners sooner and accelerate the path toward a manufacturable solution. In that sense, materials co-innovation in semiconductors is becoming as much a strategic capability as a technical one. Where the next materials transitions may occur The emerging challenges around AI illustrate why this model matters. One example is the transition from wet to dry processes for increasingly fine-pitch semiconductor structures. Continued device miniaturization can require new precursors for thin-film deposition, creating a materials challenge that combines molecular design, computational screening and process expertise. Fine-pitch precursor development is an example of this intersection between performance requirements, simulation and collaborative process development. But AI semiconductor materials requirements extend well beyond transistor fabrication. Data movement is becoming a major constraint on computing performance and energy consumption. As electrical signaling speeds increase, power requirements rise sharply, strengthening the case for optical circuits and photonic interconnects. Optical circuits are a route to significantly reducing data-center power consumption, while high-speed optical modulation is becoming critical to scaling interconnect bandwidth. These architectures create new materials opportunities—from transparent optical waveguide materials to organic electro-optic materials capable of extremely high-speed signal conversion. events.title: AI’s Storage Problem Is a Packaging Problem
events.summary: Most conversations about AI start and end with compute. But every training run and every inference query is ultimately a data problem, and data must live somewhere. Memory, and increasingly, the packaging that makes dense memory manufacturable, is doing as much to define AI system performance as the accelerators getting all the attention. AI models, cloud services, smart devices and connected systems create, process and store information at rates that would have seemed implausible a decade ago. Storage has quietly become foundational infrastructure. Consumer devices generate data continuously, from sensors to entertainment platforms. Automotive systems, particularly autonomous and connected vehicles, depend on massive volumes of stored information simply to operate safely. The result is structural, long-term demand for NAND flash rather than another consumer-driven cycle. The everyday math of a data-hungry world The growth is easy to see in ordinary digital experiences. Moving a two-hour movie from HD (1080p) to 4K increases the data required by roughly 4.7X, driven by pixel density, the added bit depth needed for HDR, and higher frame-rate targets. Photography tells a similar story: image file sizes have grown about 3X as smartphone cameras went from 12MP to 48MP, with enhanced color processing and expanded dynamic range compounding the effect. Audio has followed, a three-minute track that can grow up to 6X moving from compressed MP3 to immersive formats such as Dolby Atmos. Codec advances help. They don’t keep pace. Memory scaling must carry the rest. AI is redrawing the memory map Yole Group’s 2024 data put the stand-alone memory market at $170 billion, a 78% year-over-year rebound after two years of decline. DRAM, including HBM, accounted for roughly 57% of revenue; NAND took 40%. Heading into 2026, AI workloads are reshaping how suppliers allocate capacity. Manufacturers are expanding production of HBM and advanced DRAM nodes, prioritizing products aligned to AI performance requirements, and accelerating HBM ramps that now represent more than 10% of the total memory market. That strengthens the HBM ecosystem, but it also constrains investment in traditional DRAM and NAND capacity. NAND demand, meanwhile, keeps broadening: data center SSDs as critical storage infrastructure for AI servers; rising SSD attach rates across PCs and laptops; higher storage tiers in premium smartphones; and automotive systems where electrification and intelligent vehicle architectures require robust solid-state storage. Diversified demand supports a stable NAND outlook through 2026, even against tighter supply. From 50 packages to one The scaling story is best told in footprint. Storing 2TB in 2010, when only planar 2D NAND existed, would have taken more than 50 eMMC chips, each in a package roughly 17 x 22 mm. 3D NAND arrived in 2013 and changed the trajectory by stacking cells vertically; by 2020, 100+ layer architectures had sharply reduced the package count needed for the same capacity. Next comes wafer-to-wafer hybrid bonding, which raises interconnect density while improving electrical performance at the wafer level. It is expected to push vertical scaling well past today’s devices, toward architectures that may eventually reach 800 to 1,000 layers through multi-wafer stacking. Combined with growing QLC adoption, higher-layer 3D NAND is enabling a single eMMC device to hit 2TB. Thin, tall and reliable: the packaging problem At the package level, mobile and enterprise SSD growth is driving denser BGA packages and faster interfaces, which in turn demand tightly integrated die stacks and controller integration. Getting dies thin enough to stack higher, without giving up yield or reliability, requires coordination across the entire flow, from wafer prep through final assembly. Wafer preparation. Modern flows are engineered for 300+ layer NAND, managing die stress and warpage to prevent cracking and chipping. Key capabilities include laser grooving, ultra-fine wafer grinding, blade or stealth dicing, and automated optical inspection for crack detection. Wafers thin from roughly 700–800 µm down to as little as 25–50 µm, at which point fine grinding, polishing and backside treatments become essential to remove subsurface micro-cracks and reduce stress concentrations. Saw streets are conditioned via laser grooving or plasma pre-cut, and techniques such as dice-before-grind (DBG) and stealth dice-before-grind (SDBG) minimize edge damage. AOI runs throughout, catching cracks before compromised dies reach assembly. Die handling. As dies gets thinner, conventional handling breaks down, literally. Specialized thin-die tooling, including needle-less pickup with precisely controlled vacuum force, is required to minimize bending and prevent fracture. Wire bond architecture. At 32+ die stacks, the challenge shifts from optimizing individual steps to managing the stack as a system. Ultra-low and ultra-long loop profiles maintain clearance in tall stacks, while extended die overhang supports stair-step and zig-zag configurations. Stair-step layouts protect wire clearance; zigzag distributes stress. Customized die attach, film-on-die (FOD), film-on-wire (FOW) or spacers, prevents die sag and preserves bond integrity in controller-under-NAND configurations without adding Z-height. All of this happens inside a shrinking Z budget dictated by end applications like smartphones. Molding and warpage control. Advanced compression molding minimizes flow-induced wire sweep and distributes pressure uniformly across tall stacks. Mold cap thickness and overall material balance must be optimized against profile targets while controlling CTE mismatch. Low-stress die-attach films, carefully selected substrates and optional EMI shielding round out the materials strategy. Inspection and data analytics. Inline inspection at key stages plus unit-level traceability create the feedback loop that sustains yield — enabling early anomaly detection, rapid correlation to materials, tools or process conditions, and faster excursion containment in high-volume production. Why the OSAT role is growing Not every NAND maker is an IDM able to own the full value chain from IP and wafer fab through final assembly and test. That gap is where OSATs matter, and in today’s geopolitical environment, globally distributed manufacturing has become a strategic asset rather than a logistics footnote. Leading OSATs support consumer, industrial and automotive customers with high-stack memory packaging, unit-level traceability, wafer-level fan-out and turnkey test. Only a limited number operate true multi-region networks. As semiconductor companies prioritize diversified, geopolitically balanced supply chains, facilities spanning Asia, Europe and the United States are becoming a differentiator. Power delivery has become a critical challenge for modern computing systems, with current-density limitations, routing congestion and the growing complexity of multi-chip architectures creating new performance and reliability concerns. This paper explores how power delivery requirements are evolving across the accelerator, rack and data center hierarchy. events.title: Virtual Fabrication Meets Stress Physics: Solving GAA Channel Non-Uniformity
events.summary: Gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors are revolutionizing sub-5-nm CMOS chips, but a subtle design challenge has come into focus: the mechanical stress created in the nanosheet channels does not distribute uniformly across stacked GAA transistors. Because stress reshapes the silicon band structure and directly changes carrier mobility, 1 even small imbalances between the stacked nanosheets can distort device behavior in ways that are difficult to predict from geometry alone. What causes stress non-uniformity in GAA transistors? Stress non-uniformity occurs when stacked nanosheet channels experience different strain levels during fabrication. These differences affect carrier mobility, current flow, threshold voltage, and leakage. Using SEMulator3D stress modeling, engineers can identify these variations early and optimize channel thickness, fin width, and lateral etch to improve performance. To illustrate, imagine that a GAA transistor’s stacked channels are three parallel highway lanes meant to carry traffic evenly. If one lane is smoother or wider than the others, more cars naturally shift into it. Similarly, if one nanosheet has higher stress and better carrier mobility, it could carry a disproportionate share of current, throwing off the device’s expected behavior. Fixing this stress problem requires a tool that can emulate a sequence of semiconductor fabrication steps and proactively identify stress problems in the resulting three-dimensional structure. Lam Semiverse Solutions engineers used SEMulator3D with integrated stress modeling to predict stress variations across GAA stacked nanosheets and learn how to improve stress uniformity. They identified how channel thickness, fin width, and lateral etch interact to drive non-uniform stress, revealing that a slightly thicker top channel dramatically improves uniformity. Why stress uniformity is critical for GAA nanosheet transistor performance Fig. 1: Gate-all-around field-effect transistor architecture. A GAA architecture consists of isolated silicon channels stacked vertically between the source and drain. The channels are wrapped by the gate, which controls electron transport and the on/off state of the transistor. Stress or strain in the channels reshapes the silicon band structure and the carrier mobility, saturation current, off-state current, and threshold voltage. Ideally, all GAA channels see identical stress and behave identically. In practice, process-induced variations cause them to see different stress or strain levels. The highest-stressed channel exhibits enhanced mobility and carries a disproportionate share of the current. A high-strain, low-Vt (threshold voltage) nanosheet channel can dominate off-state leakage, even if the other channels remain well controlled. This leakage current can create a spread in Vt and modify the effective turn-on characteristic of the transistor in unexpected ways. Uniform stress across the stack is therefore a critical design target, and simulation is essential because it is not obvious at the outset how to achieve it. Simulate stress in GAA nanosheet devices We created a 3D process model of the GAA device by inputting layout, process step, 2,3 and material information into SEMulator3D. We then explored predicted stress levels in the GAA channels using the generated 3D model with integrated stress analysis. Stress is generated in the channels because of lattice mismatch between silicon and the epitaxially grown source and drain regions. For the pFET, the epitaxially grown source/drain material has a slightly greater lattice constant than silicon. The nFET source/drain material has a slightly smaller lattice constant than silicon. During the replacement-metal-gate (RMG) process steps, the channels become freestanding, which allows these stressors to relax. The compressively stressed source/drain regions expand and push the pFET channels into compression, while the tensile stressed source/drain regions contract and pull the nFET channels into tension (see Figure 2). Fig. 2: Stress transfer to the silicon channel during the fabrication process. In the model, stress is solved during every major process step change: the epitaxial Si/SiGe stack, fin patterning, the gate module, source/drain growth, and the RMG module. How channel thickness influences stress uniformity in GAA nanosheets We executed a Design of Experiments (DOE) to test the impact of design changes on stress uniformity. The DOE varied the individual silicon layer thicknesses (Channel 1 to 3 thickness) and the fin width. Together, these parameters control the channel cross-section area, the primary driver of stress. We extracted the average longitudinal stress (Sigma_yy) along a vertical cut of the channels (Figure 3). Three clear peaks of stress magnitude are shown, which correspond to the three nanosheets used in our model. These stress peaks are compressive for the pFET and tensile for the nFET. The three values are visibly different, with the nFET demonstrating larger stress non-uniformity or variability. Fig. 3: Control parameters for the DoE and the Sigma_yy along the z-cut of the channels for both pFET and nFET. Figure 4 represents stress non-uniformity (referred to as “stress difference”) using a contour plot as a function of the DOE variables. The stress difference for the pFET stays under 200 MPa, while the nFET stress difference reaches 400 to 800 MPa. The stress difference is most sensitive to the topmost channel’s (Channel 3) thickness. As Channel 3’s thickness increases, the stress difference decreases. This is seen in Figure 4, as Channel 3’s thickness increases from 4 nm to 7 nm, and the red (highest stress difference) contours change to blue (lowest stress difference). This result indicates that the topmost channel (Channel 3) needs to be slightly thicker than the channels below to minimize the stress difference among channels. Fig. 4: Top channel thickness contributes most to stress non-uniformity. How fin width and lateral etch affect GAA stress uniformity The impact of fin width becomes pronounced when the fin lateral-etch ratio is high (Figure 5). The fin width is measured at the shallow trench isolation (STI) elevation for reference. The fin lateral etch ratio controls the fin taper and determines the channel width loss above the STI elevation. Fig. 5: The impact of fin lateral etch on the channel width. At a low lateral etch ratio, the fin taper is low, and channel width variation is not significant. At high lateral etch, the top channel becomes significantly narrower than the bottom. The interaction of fin width and fin lateral etch, for stress non-uniformity, is seen in Figure 6. At a lower lateral etch ratio of 0.05 and 0.075, the stress difference contours do not change much as the fin width is reduced. events.title: From Silicon To Systems: Heterogeneous Integration As The Engine Of AI Performance
events.summary: We are in the middle of one of the most important shifts our industry has seen in decades. The internet economy transformed how people connect, communicate, and consume information. The AI economy is redefining a more fundamental layer: how compute is architected, delivered, scaled, and optimized. AI workloads are creating demands for power, memory bandwidth, I/O, thermal performance, and system-level efficiency that traditional silicon scaling alone cannot satisfy. In my SKYTalk at the Design Automation Conference (DAC) 2026, I shared that meeting this moment requires expanding our frame of innovation beyond silicon alone to the full system: silicon, package, board, platform, software, and the ecosystem that brings them together. Through 18 papers and posters at the conference, our Intel engineers showcased research spanning advanced packaging, AI-enabled design, verification, and system technology co-optimization (STCO), highlighting innovations that help optimize and scale increasingly complex 3DIC, chiplet-based, and heterogeneous systems. Advanced packaging becomes an architectural foundation This shift is putting advanced packaging at the center of the next era of performance. For many years, packaging was viewed primarily as the final step in semiconductor manufacturing to protect the die, connect it to the board, and help remove heat. That role has changed dramatically. Today, advanced packaging is no longer just an integration step. It is becoming an architectural foundation. It enables us to connect chiplets, integrate memory and high-speed I/O, manage power and thermals, and build systems that would not be practical or possible as monolithic silicon. The industry has already embraced chiplets and heterogeneous integration as powerful tools. By disaggregating a monolithic design into functional chiplets, we can mix and match design blocks, process nodes, foundries, and technologies to optimize performance, cost, yield, and time to market. This approach enables products that can exceed reticle limits, reuse IP more efficiently, and align each function with the process technology best suited to its requirements. But chiplets alone are not the end goal. The real opportunity comes when we move beyond a chiplet mindset to a systems mindset. For AI, this systems mindset is essential. AI architectures do not allow us to optimize the die, package, and board in isolation. The performance vectors are too interdependent. Thermal behavior influences architecture choices. Power delivery affects performance headroom. Mechanical constraints affect yield and reliability. Memory integration and high-speed I/O affect the entire product landing zone. If we cannot model, explore, verify, and close these interactions across silicon, package, and system, we do not fully unlock the value of the technologies we are developing. Technology opens possibilities. Design enablement creates reality. Design space exploration in the AI era This is why design space exploration must become a core capability for advanced packaging and chiplet-based systems. It provides a structured way to evaluate architectural trade-offs and identify the optimal product landing zone using validated models, tools, and methodologies. It spans decisions across architecture, connectivity, packaging, and manufacturing. Teams must determine how functionality should be partitioned, which process technologies to use, and how dies will communicate within the package. At the same time, they need to balance system-level considerations such as power delivery, thermal performance, memory integration, and high-speed I/O while ensuring the design can be manufactured and scaled with strong yield. None of these choices can be made independently. The value comes from understanding the trade-offs early, before the cost of change becomes too high. A key example is die-to-die IP. Chiplet architectures depend on physical and functional connectivity between dies, and that connectivity must be co-designed with the package. Success depends on getting details right, from bump pitch and bump maps to package compatibility, electrical performance, and validation using real test silicon. Looking beyond a single product, widespread chiplet adoption will require a much broader ecosystem. Interoperable die-to-die IP, package technologies, process nodes, foundries, design kits, standards, and IP providers must work together seamlessly. Interoperability is not a nice-to-have. It is a requirement if we want heterogeneous integration to scale. Thermals and mechanics are another example of why system-level optimization is now mandatory. AI workloads can sustain near-peak activity, creating new thermal challenges and localized hot spots. On-package integration increases power density, and the package must increasingly support thermal strategies that reach into the system level. That means thermal analysis must happen early, beginning at architecture definition, and continue through IP planning, silicon floorplanning, package layout, and system design. Experimentally calibrated models, material characterization, and continuous feedback are essential to making those analyses accurate and actionable. Power delivery must be treated with the same level of system thinking. Performance headroom starts in the package. The placement of decoupling capacitance and other power delivery ingredients across die, package, and system have a direct impact on product capability. As these systems grow more complex, connecting physical understanding with design enablement becomes increasingly critical. From sequential design to concurrent system co-optimization These challenges also expose the limitations of the traditional sequential design model. Historically, chip, package, and board teams could work in a largely serial flow, synchronizing at key boundaries such as bump maps and package footprints. That model breaks down for AI systems. Today, we need concurrent design across chiplets, package, board, and system. We must optimize together for performance, cost, yield, time to market, form factor, reliability, and manufacturability. The package cannot be treated as a downstream constraint. It must be part of the architecture from the start. Enabling that level of concurrent optimization requires more sophisticated modeling and simulation capabilities than traditional design flows can provide. Fig. 1: Advanced packaging increasingly relies on concurrent co-design and verification across silicon, package, and board domains. Digital twins and multiphysics modeling will be increasingly important in this transformation. As systems become larger and more complex, we need better ways to predict outcomes, compare configurations, and reduce risk before committing to expensive prototypes. events.title: Predicting Silicon Behavior Years Before Test Wafers
events.summary: Semiconductor engineers have known for decades that serial fabrication runs of test wafers is an inefficient way to bring up new processes and technologies. Modern deep submicron nodes have only reinforced this observation. It now costs several years and tens of billions of dollars just to build a fab. Every test wafer run takes months and costs millions. Finding problems after a run, figuring out the causes, devising fixes, and waiting for the next set of wafers to confirm the results is just not feasible anymore. The only solution is an electronic design automation (EDA) toolset that can accurately predict chip behavior before any wafers are run, and even before the fab is ready. This enables the very first test wafers to closely match the desired characteristics. It also minimizes the number of tweaks and fab runs needed to refine the process for production designs. Synopsys S-Litho , which provides early lithography pathfinding, process optimization, and analysis, is a prime example of such a solution. Recent results demonstrate dramatically the accuracy of its predictions years before test wafers are available. A prediction case study In 2021, Synopsys engineers used S-Litho to simulate high-NA (numerical aperture) EUV (extreme ultraviolet) lithography for a 22nm pitch. The analysis predicted about a 0.5 nm line width roughness (LWR) for horizontal (H) compared with vertical (V). Since line edge roughness (LER) is generally a bit more than half of LWR, the LER prediction was therefore around 0.3 nm for H compared to V. S-Litho also predicted a 50% failure rate reduction for H versus V lines. These predictions were published in May 2021 in the Journal of Micro/Nanopatterning, Materials, and Metrology 1 : The prediction that vertical lines would have higher defectivity and LER than horizontal lines meant that lines would come out jagged instead of smooth, and even small deviations would impact performance greatly. Frankly, there was considerable industry skepticism at the time about these conclusions. Past experience had shown that in low-NA EUV lithography, horizontal lines exhibited higher defectivity and worse LER than vertical lines. At the time, not only were wafer results unavailable, but wafer fab equipment (WFE) was still in development. In fact, WFE manufacturers were among the skeptics. Silicon results It took several years for equipment to be developed, fabs to be built, and test wafers to be run. Actual 21 nm silicon results were presented by IBM at the International Conference on Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography 2 in 2025 and at Optical and EUV Nanolithography XXXIX 3 in 2026. These results showed that vertical lines had LER of 1.6 nm and horizontal lines LER of 1.3 nm, the 0.3 nm difference predicted four years earlier by S-Litho. The graphs below show the reported LER measurements for horizontal lines on the left and vertical lines on the right. In 21/22 nm high-NA EUV, the horizontal direction is illuminated at an angle, the Chief Ray Angle. This is necessary to use the Bragg reflector and keep the incoming and outgoing photons from interfering. Also, the illumination angle needs to be below roughly 12 degrees to keep the reflected intensity as high as possible. The horizontal direction has an 8X magnification, and the vertical direction has a 4X magnification. Industry opinion in 2021 was that shadowing would degrade the horizontal direction performance, as observed in 0.33 NA EUV, where the vertical direction has better performance than the horizontal, but both have 4X magnification. The magnification impact on LER was thought to be less than the shadowing impact. Contrary to expectations, in high-NA EUV the magnification dominated, which S-Litho correctly predicted. Benefits of prediction S-Litho provides physics-based, end-to-end lithography simulation independent of WFE development and long before test wafer results. The IBM silicon measurements testify to the accuracy of S-Litho LER predictions. IBM could not (yet) report real-world failure rates since it takes millions of parts in production to establish a failure history. The ability of S-Litho to predict failure rates before test wafers, let alone full production, is highly valuable. S-Litho’s power and accuracy have important benefits for the semiconductor industry. For advanced nodes with high-NA EUV lithography, early, trusted prediction reduces risk and guides process and design tradeoffs. It also informs the selection of hardware and software development tools. Accurate predictive simulation is a prerequisite for technology leadership. These results also have positive implications for Synopsys Proteus full-chip mask synthesis smart manufacturing solutions. High-NA Proteus OPC (Optical Proximity Correction) was built and validated using S-Litho. Thus, chip developers can also count on Proteus results before silicon is available. The number of test wafer runs is dramatically reduced. If process tweaks are made, S-Litho can check to see if the desired effects will be achieved without waiting for a new fab run. As fab times continue to elongate, any reduction in test wafer runs saves enormous time and cost. Conclusion The ability to predict future lithography behavior has become a strategic enabler for semiconductor development. S-Litho is the first wafer-validated optical simulation solution for high-NA EUV applications. Process developers no longer have to wait for next-generation equipment or fabs. S-Litho is a key step toward the industry goal of having true digital twins for processes. Learn more about S-Litho Predictive Lithography Simulation .
